title: Simplify Path
description: A direct, already-optimal stack-based simulation: split the path into tokens, then skip, pop, or push based on each token's exact value.

blocks.text: Given an absolute Unix-style file path, convert it to its SIMPLIFIED canonical form. Rules: multiple consecutive slashes are treated as one; a single period "." refers to the current directory (and is ignored); a double period ".." refers to the parent directory (going up one level, but never above the root); the canonical path must start with a single slash, and directories are separated by exactly one slash, with no trailing slash (except the root itself, "/").

blocks.caption: A stack of directory names directly models the canonical path: ".." pops (goes up), "." and empty segments are ignored, real names push

blocks.text: Splitting the path on "/" produces a sequence of tokens, most of which are genuine directory names to descend into; ".." tokens should instead remove the most recently entered directory (never going above the root), and "." tokens (along with any empty tokens from repeated or trailing slashes) contribute nothing at all.

blocks.title: Analogy: Following Written Directions Through a Building, Including "Go Back" Instructions
blocks.text: Imagine following a written list of directions through a building: most instructions say "enter room X" (walk deeper), some say "stay where you are" (do nothing), and some say "go back to the room you were just in" (retrace one step). A stack of "rooms visited so far" directly tracks the current position: entering a room pushes it, going back pops the most recent one, and staying in place does nothing at all.

blocks.caption: Splitting the path on "/" produces tokens; each is classified as ignorable, a pop instruction, or a genuine directory name to push

blocks.text: Before manually tracking string manipulation for merging slashes and resolving "..", notice that splitting the path into tokens and processing each one against a stack directly and cleanly handles every rule at once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Splitting the path string on "/" directly handles the "multiple consecutive slashes" rule for free, since consecutive slashes produce EMPTY tokens between them, which can simply be filtered out.

Observation 2: A "." token means "stay in the current directory," contributing nothing to the canonical path, so it too can simply be skipped.

Observation 3: A ".." token means "go up one level," which is exactly a stack pop, with the natural safeguard of doing nothing if the stack is already empty (already at the root, cannot go higher).

Observation 4: Any other (non-empty, non-"." , non-"..") token is a genuine directory or file name, simply pushed onto the stack.

Observation 5: After processing every token, the final canonical path is reconstructed by joining the stack's contents with "/", prefixed by a single leading "/".
This is a direct stack-based simulation: split the path into tokens, and let each token's type (empty/".", "..", or a real name) determine whether it is ignored, triggers a pop, or is pushed.
Split the path on "/" into tokens, then walk through them, classifying and handling each one directly against a growing result list.

items: Split the path string on "/" to get a list of tokens (some of which may be empty, due to consecutive or trailing slashes).
For each token: skip if empty or ".", pop the result list if "..", otherwise append the token to the result list.
Join the result list with "/", prefixed by a leading "/", to form the canonical path.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Splitting on "/" directly leverages the language's built-in string splitting, automatically producing empty tokens between consecutive slashes, which are then simply filtered.
A stack-like list naturally supports both appending (descending) and removing-the-last-element (going up) operations needed here.

blocks.text: Correctly resolves every path-simplification rule, since each token is classified and handled exactly according to the problem's specification.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass over the tokens (splitting itself is also O(n)).
Space: O(n), for the token list and the result stack.

This IS already the natural and optimal approach for this problem; there is no meaningfully "slower" naive alternative worth comparing against, since a stack-based single pass directly and efficiently matches the problem's structure.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since the direct stack-based token-processing approach already achieves O(n) time and correctly handles every rule, "optimizing" here means ensuring the implementation is clean and correctly handles every edge case: repeated slashes, trailing slashes, "." segments, and ".." at (or above) the root.
Split the path on "/". For each token: if empty or ".", skip it; if "..", pop the stack if it is non-empty; otherwise, push the token. Join the final stack with "/", prefixed by a leading "/".
Process each token from splitting the path against a stack, letting the token's type determine whether it is skipped, pops, or pushes.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: "/" + "".../b/d" = "/.../b/d", matching the expected result: "..." is treated as an ordinary directory name here, not a special token.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

Only the EXACT strings "." and ".." carry special meaning; any other token (including unusual-looking ones like "..." with three dots) is treated as a genuine, ordinary directory or file name, correctly pushed onto the stack. Splitting on "/" and filtering empty tokens elegantly absorbs both repeated internal slashes and any trailing slash, without needing separate special-case handling for either.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A token is empty (from // or a trailing /)","Skipped entirely, contributing nothing"],["A token is exactly \".\"","Skipped (stay in the current directory)"],["A token is exactly \"..\"","Pops the stack (go up one level), or does nothing if already at the root"],["Any other token","Pushed as a genuine directory/file name"]]}

items: The equality checks (token === "." or token === "..") must be EXACT string matches, correctly distinguishing them from superficially similar but different names like "..." or ".hidden".
The final join with "/" and a leading "/" correctly reconstructs the canonical path format, including the special case of an empty stack producing just "/" (the root).
No trailing slash is ever added, since the join operation only places "/" BETWEEN elements, never after the last one.

blocks.text: Simplifying a file system path is a direct stack simulation: splitting on the path separator naturally produces the tokens to process, and a stack elegantly models "descend" (push) versus "go back up" (pop) navigation, with "." and empty tokens simply filtered out.

items: Using a substring or "contains" check for "." or ".." instead of an EXACT equality check, incorrectly treating names like "..." or ".config" as special tokens.
Forgetting the safeguard against popping an already-empty stack, which would error out (or need special handling) for a ".." at the root.
Adding a trailing slash to the final result, which the canonical format explicitly disallows (except for the root path itself).

items: Explicitly stating "only the EXACT tokens '.' and '..' are special; everything else, however unusual it looks, is a real name" heads off a common misunderstanding about names like "..." early.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Simplify/canonicalize a file system path" points directly to a stack-based token simulation: split on the separator, then push/pop/skip based on each token's exact value.

items: How would you handle a RELATIVE path (not starting with "/") instead? The same token-processing logic applies, but the final joined result would not be prefixed with a leading "/", and ".." at the very start would need to be preserved literally (since there is no absolute root to safely discard it against).

How would you extend this to Windows-style paths (using "\\" as the separator, and drive letters)? The core stack logic remains the same; only the splitting/joining separator and a small amount of drive-letter-specific handling would need to change.
What is the maximum possible stack size, and when does it occur? Proportional to the number of genuine directory names in the path, occurring when there are no ".." tokens to reduce it.

A direct stack-based simulation, conceptually related to Crawler Log Folder elsewhere in this category, though that problem only ever needs the final DEPTH (a counter suffices), while this one needs the actual resulting PATH (requiring a true stack of names).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: O(n) time, O(n) space: a single stack-based pass, already optimal for this problem.

items: Pattern: Direct stack-based path token simulation
Core Idea: Split the path on "/"; skip empty and "." tokens, pop on "..", push any other token as a genuine directory name; join the final stack with "/"
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Only the EXACT tokens "." and ".." are special; anything else (however unusual, like "...") is a genuine name to push
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Split on "/"; skip "" and ".", pop on "..", push everything else; join with "/"
